Penguin Species Classification

Author

Yuxue (Jade) Zhu, Maxine Paredes, Abhishek Sharma, Hephzibah Adeniji

Published

November 19, 2026

from pathlib import Path
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
import altair as alt
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    precision_score,
    recall_score,
    f1_score,
    confusion_matrix,
)
# png, so the charts also show in the PDF
_ = alt.renderers.enable("png", scale_factor=2)

Summary

In this analysis, we ask whether flipper length or body mass more accurately classifies penguin species (Adélie, Chinstrap, or Gentoo). To answer this, we built two classification models using the logistic regression algorithm, each of which independently used one of these body measurements from penguins in the Palmer Archipelago region to predict species. On an unseen test data set, the flipper length model outperformed the body mass model on every metric, with an overall accuracy of 0.837 compared with 0.744, and a macro F1-score of 0.715 compared with 0.561. For both models, macro recall and F1-score were well below overall accuracy, meaning that performance was uneven across species: Gentoo penguins, which are noticeably larger, were easy to identify, while the similarly sized Adélie and Chinstrap penguins were often confused. These results suggest that a stable structural trait such as flipper length captures species differences better than body mass, which varies with a penguin’s condition. As a result, although flipper length is the more informative of the two measurements, we do not believe that either one alone is enough to reliably distinguish all three species. Our analysis is also limited by its small, imbalanced data set (only 68 Chinstrap penguins), collected from a single region over three breeding seasons, so the results may not generalise to other populations or years. Further research combining several measurements, such as bill length and depth, is needed to separate Adélie and Chinstrap penguins more reliably.

Introduction

Background

The Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst et al., 2022) contains body measurements of adult Adélie, Chinstrap and Gentoo penguins (genus Pygoscelis) nesting on three islands in Antarctica’s Palmer Archipelago: Biscoe, Dream and Torgersen. The data was collected from 2007 to 2009 by Dr. Kristen Gorman and the Palmer Station Antarctica Long Term Ecological Research (LTER) program, as part of a study of differences between male and female penguins (Gorman et al., 2014).

Every breeding season, researchers identified nests where pairs of adults were present prior to egg-laying and consistently monitored these sites. Once a nest was found to have one egg, both adults were captured, measured, and had a blood sample taken to determine each penguin’s sex (Gorman et al., 2014). Consequently, every observation in the data set represents a breeding adult measured at the same point in the nesting cycle.

Research Question

Does flipper length or body mass more accurately classify penguin species (Adélie, Chinstrap, Gentoo)?

Relevance

Exploring how flipper length and body mass independently relates to penguin species is valuable because the two measurements describe very different kinds of traits. Flipper length is structural: once a penguin is fully grown, it stays roughly constant. In comparison, body mass varies based on factors like foraging success (Emmerson et al., 2019) and breeding effort (Chappell et al., 1993), so it reflects a penguin’s current condition as much as its species. Finding out which one better separates the species tells us whether species differences are better captured by stable body structure or by size that fluctuates, which matters for any study that compares penguins measured at different times or under different conditions.

Data Description

We use the penguins data set from the palmerpenguins package (Horst et al., 2022), which contains 344 penguins: 152 Adélie, 68 Chinstrap and 124 Gentoo. Each row represents one adult penguin and records its species, island, bill length, bill depth, flipper length, body mass, sex and study year. Our analysis uses three of these variables:

  • Species (Adélie, Chinstrap or Gentoo): the target we classify.
  • Flipper length, in millimetres.
  • Body mass, in grams.

Two penguins have no flipper length or body mass recorded, so we remove them before analysis. The remaining variables are not used.

Methods

Data Collection

We used the Palmer Penguins dataset, which contains measurements and species information for penguins observed in the Palmer Archipelago, Antarctica. The dataset was obtained from the publicly available GitHub repository maintained by the Palmer Penguins project (Horst et al., 2022).

We focused on three variables: penguin species, flipper length, and body mass. Species was used as the response variable, while flipper length and body mass were evaluated separately as predictors.

# Create data directories
raw_dir = Path("../data/raw")
processed_dir = Path("../data/processed")

raw_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
processed_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Download the original dataset
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/allisonhorst/palmerpenguins/main/inst/extdata/penguins.csv"
raw_data = pd.read_csv(url)

# Save the original dataset
raw_data.to_csv(raw_dir / "penguins.csv", index=False)

# Select relevant variables and remove missing values
data = raw_data[
    ["species", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"]
].dropna()

# Save processed data
data.to_csv(processed_dir / "penguins_cleaned.csv", index=False)

Train-Test Splitting

We divided the cleaned dataset into training and testing sets using a 75:25 ratio. We performed this split before exploratory data analysis and preprocessing to prevent information from the test set from influencing model development.

train_data, test_data = train_test_split(
    data,
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=123,
    stratify=data["species"]
)
train_data.to_csv(processed_dir / "penguins_train.csv", index=False)
test_data.to_csv(processed_dir / "penguins_test.csv", index=False)

# Separate response variable and predictors
y_train = train_data["species"]
y_test = test_data["species"]

X_train_flipper = train_data[["flipper_length_mm"]]
X_test_flipper = test_data[["flipper_length_mm"]]

X_train_mass = train_data[["body_mass_g"]]
X_test_mass = test_data[["body_mass_g"]]

Exploratory Data Analysis

We explored the training data to understand how flipper length and body mass vary across the three penguin species. We calculated descriptive statistics (Table 1) and created boxplots (Figure 1 and Figure 2) to examine differences between species and identify potential overlap in their measurements.

# Descriptive statistics, with readable column names
summary_stats = (
    train_data.groupby("species")
    .agg(**{
        "Number of Penguins": ("species", "size"),
        "Mean Flipper Length (mm)": ("flipper_length_mm", "mean"),
        "SD Flipper Length (mm)": ("flipper_length_mm", "std"),
        "Mean Body Mass (g)": ("body_mass_g", "mean"),
        "SD Body Mass (g)": ("body_mass_g", "std"),
    })
    .reset_index()
    .rename(columns={"species": "Species"})
)
summary_stats.style.hide(axis="index").format(precision=2)

# Visualize measurements by species
# Flipper length by species
flipper_chart = alt.Chart(train_data).mark_boxplot().encode(
    y=alt.Y("species:N", title="Penguin Species"),
    x=alt.X("flipper_length_mm:Q", title="Flipper Length (mm)").scale(zero=False),
    color=alt.Color("species:N", title="Species")
).properties(
    title="Flipper Length by Penguin Species"
)
flipper_chart
# Body mass by species
mass_chart = alt.Chart(train_data).mark_boxplot().encode(
    y=alt.Y("species:N", title="Penguin Species"),
    x=alt.X("body_mass_g:Q", title="Body Mass (g)").scale(zero=False),
    color=alt.Color("species:N", title="Species")
).properties(
    title="Body Mass by Penguin Species"
)
mass_chart

To investigate whether flipper length or body mass is more effective at classifying penguin species, we compared the mean and standard deviation of each feature across the three species (Table 1).

Gentoo penguins have the longest mean flipper length (217.45 mm) and the highest mean body mass (5100.27 g), making them distinct from the other two species (Figure 1 and Figure 2). In contrast, Adélie and Chinstrap penguins have more similar measurements, with mean flipper lengths of 189.77 mm and 196.41 mm, and mean body masses of 3700.44 g and 3745.10 g, respectively.

Flipper length has relatively low within-species variability (standard deviations ranging from 6.41 to 7.48 mm), while body mass shows greater variability (standard deviations ranging from 415.03 to 508.32 g). This suggests that flipper length may provide more consistent information for distinguishing species. However, the summary statistics alone cannot determine which feature classifies species more accurately, particularly for Adélie and Chinstrap penguins, whose measurements overlap.

Therefore, we will compare the classification performance of models using flipper length and body mass separately, and evaluate their accuracy to determine which feature better predicts penguin species.

Model Training

We used logistic regression to classify penguins into three species: Adélie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo. Logistic regression is a classification method that estimates the probability of an observation belonging to each category (Hosmer et al., 2013), which suits our question because it gives a simple, interpretable model for a single numeric predictor.

To compare the predictive ability of the two measurements, we developed two separate models:

  • Flipper length model: uses flipper length as the only predictor.
  • Body mass model: uses body mass as the only predictor.

Both models used the same training and testing sets. Within each model pipeline, we standardized the predictor (rescaled it to have a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one) before fitting. Because the scaling is part of the pipeline, its parameters are learned from the training data only.

# Model 1: Flipper length
flipper_model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
)

flipper_model.fit(X_train_flipper, y_train);
# Model 2: Body mass
mass_model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
)

mass_model.fit(X_train_mass, y_train);

Model Evaluation

We evaluated both models using accuracy and macro-averaged F1-score on the test set. Accuracy measures the proportion of correctly classified penguins. However, because the number of observations may differ across species, accuracy alone may not fully represent classification performance.

The macro-averaged F1-score considers both precision and recall and calculates the average F1-score across all three species, giving each species equal weight. This allows us to assess how well each model performs across the different classes.

We also used confusion matrices to examine which species were correctly classified and which were misclassified.

# Generate test-set predictions using the fitted pipelines
y_pred_flipper = flipper_model.predict(X_test_flipper)
y_pred_mass = mass_model.predict(X_test_mass)

# Build clean summary comparison table
results_table = pd.DataFrame({
    "Predictor": ["Flipper Length", "Body Mass"],
    "Overall Accuracy": [
        round(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_flipper), 3),
        round(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_mass), 3),
    ],
    "Macro Precision": [
        round(precision_score(y_test, y_pred_flipper, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
        round(precision_score(y_test, y_pred_mass, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
    ],
    "Macro Recall": [
        round(recall_score(y_test, y_pred_flipper, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
        round(recall_score(y_test, y_pred_mass, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
    ],
    "Macro F1-Score": [
        round(f1_score(y_test, y_pred_flipper, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
        round(f1_score(y_test, y_pred_mass, average="macro", zero_division=0), 3),
    ],
})
results_table
Predictor Overall Accuracy Macro Precision Macro Recall Macro F1-Score

Results

To evaluate whether flipper length or body mass more accurately classifies penguin species, both fitted logistic regression models were evaluated on the held-out test set (\(n = 86\)). Table 2 compares the overall test accuracy alongside macro averaged precision, recall, and F1-score for each single-predictor model.

})

Body Mass 0.744 0.525 0.617 0.561

Table 2. Held-out test set classification performance comparing single-predictor logistic regression models using flipper length versus body mass across overall accuracy and macro averaged precision, recall, and F1-score.

As shown in Table 2, flipper length outperformed body mass across every evaluation metric. The flipper length classifier achieved an overall test accuracy of 0.837 and a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.715, compared to an overall accuracy of 0.744 and a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.561 for the body mass classifier.

species_order = ["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"]

def build_cm_df(y_true, y_pred, model_label):
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, labels=species_order)
    rows = []
    for i, actual in enumerate(species_order):
        for j, predicted in enumerate(species_order):
            rows.append({
                "Model": model_label,
                "Actual Species": actual,
                "Predicted Species": predicted,
                "Count": int(cm[i, j]),
            })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

cm_combined = pd.concat([
    build_cm_df(y_test, y_pred_flipper, "Flipper Length Model"),
    build_cm_df(y_test, y_pred_mass, "Body Mass Model"),
], ignore_index=True)

base = alt.Chart(cm_combined).encode(
    x=alt.X("Predicted Species:N", sort=species_order, title="Predicted Species"),
    y=alt.Y("Actual Species:N", sort=species_order, title="Actual Species"),
)

heatmap = base.mark_rect().encode(
    color=alt.Color("Count:Q", scale=alt.Scale(scheme="blues"), title="Penguin Count")
)

text = base.mark_text(fontSize=13, fontWeight="bold").encode(
    text="Count:Q",
    color=alt.condition(
        alt.datum.Count > 15,
        alt.value("white"),
        alt.value("black"),
    ),
)

cm_chart = (heatmap + text).properties(
    width=220,
    height=220,
).facet(
    column=alt.Column(
        "Model:N",
        sort=["Flipper Length Model", "Body Mass Model"],
        title=None,
        header=alt.Header(labelFontSize=13, labelFontWeight="bold"),
    )
).configure_axis(
    labelFontSize=11,
    titleFontSize=12,
)

cm_chart

Figure 3. Side-by-side confusion matrices comparing actual versus predicted penguin species on the held-out test set for the flipper length logistic regression model (left) and the body mass logistic regression model (right).

Figure 3 illustrates how each predictor separates the three penguin species on the test set. Both models reliably identified Gentoo penguins, reflecting their noticeably longer flippers and larger body mass relative to the other two species. However, substantial overlap between Adélie and Chinstrap penguins limited single feature classification performance, with the body mass model misclassifying almost all Chinstrap penguins as Adélie, whereas flipper length provided moderately stronger separation between those two smaller species.

Discussion

Pygoscelis adeliae (Adélie), Pygoscelis papua (Gentoo), and Pygoscelis antarcticus (Chinstrap) are three species of brush-tailed penguins residing in the Antarctic. Using the Palmer Penguins dataset (Horst et al., 2022), we considered which trait (flipper length or body mass) is a better predictive feature to classify a penguin’s species.

Prior to fitting the model, we expected flipper length to be a better predictor of penguin species. This was because biologically, flippers are more distinct anatomical structures of a penguin that can mark evolutionary ancestry (hence species differentiation), compared to a flexible trait like body mass (Bels et al., 2026). Also, our exploratory data analysis showed a large overlap in the body mass of Adélie and Chinstrap penguins, and we expected the machine learning model to have a harder time distinguishing between those two species.

Our held-out test set results with logistic regression demonstrate that flipper length is a substantially stronger single predictor of Palmer penguin species than body mass. Flipper length achieved an overall test accuracy of 0.837 and a macro-averaged F1-score of 0.715 compared to 0.744 accuracy and a 0.561 macro-averaged F1-score for body mass. This performance gap aligns with biological differences between structural skeletal traits and pliable physiological traits in the seabirds.  Once adult penguins reach maturity, flipper length typically remains relatively stable across the breeding season, providing a consistent morphological signal across species. By contrast, body mass can fluctuate considerably depending on recent foraging success, fasting during incubation, and parental provisioning duties (Gorman et al., 2014), introducing within species variance that blurs decision boundaries in a single-predictor logistic regression model.

Examining species-level errors reveals why overall accuracy remained below 0.85 for both single-feature classifiers. Gentoo penguins are noticeably larger in both flipper length and body mass than their congeners in the Palmer Archipelago, allowing both models to identify Gentoo individuals with high reliability. However, Adélie and Chinstrap penguins share very similar body mass distributions, causing the body mass classifier to misclassify nearly all test-set Chinstrap penguins as Adélie. While flipper length separated Adélie and Chinstrap penguins moderately better than body mass, a single linear boundary on one morphological feature cannot fully resolve overlapping measurements between these two smaller species.

Several limitations should be considered when interpreting these findings. First, restricting each logistic regression model to a single predictor ignores complementary morphological traits such as bill length and bill depth that strongly distinguish Chinstrap penguins from Adélie penguins. Second, the dataset exhibits class imbalance across species and spans three breeding seasons across different islands in the Palmer Archipelago (Horst et al., 2022), meaning environmental and inter-annual shifts in prey availability could influence body mass measurements. Third, adult penguins exhibit sexual dimorphism in body size (Gorman et al., 2014), and pooling males and females without accounting for sex increases overlap between smaller males of one species and larger females of another. In addition, this classification is based purely on machine learning and cannot cover the scope of correct taxonomic classification of a species.

Future analyses could extend this work in three practical directions. First, fitting a multivariable logistic regression model or regularized classifier that combines flipper length with bill length and bill depth would quantify how much classification accuracy improves when structural bill morphology is included alongside flipper length. Second, incorporating penguin sex and nesting island as covariates or interaction terms could clarify whether accounting for sexual dimorphism resolves the remaining confusion between Adélie and Chinstrap penguins. Finally, evaluating non-linear classifiers such as random forests or support vector machines on the multi-feature dataset could test whether curved decision boundaries capture subtle morphological separation across all three species.
